questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: A `static` local variable is initialised once and keeps its value between calls, so the counter goes 1, 2, 3.
option_notes: That would be an ordinary local variable (re-initialised on every call), but here it is static.
Correct: the static variable survives between calls.
It starts at 0 but is incremented before it is returned (`++n`).
Nothing makes the three calls return the same value.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `size_t` are true?
options: It is an unsigned integer type
It is the type of the result of `sizeof`
It can hold the size of the largest object the system can address
questions.explain: `size_t` is an unsigned type chosen by the implementation to hold object sizes. On a 64-bit system it is typically 8 bytes, so it is not always 4. Print it with `%zu`.
option_notes: False: it is typically 8 bytes on 64-bit systems.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates an `int` variable called `count` with the initial value 10?
questions.explain: A declaration is `type name = value;`. `==` is the comparison operator, and C has no `integer` type.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `int b = a;` copies the VALUE of `a` at that moment. Changing `a` afterwards does not affect `b`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: An `unsigned char` holds 0 to 255. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around (it is well defined): 255 + 1 becomes 0.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: A `char` is a small integer: 'A' is 65, so `c + 2` is 67, which `%c` prints as `C`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (Careful with the division.)
questions.explain: `7 / 2` is an INTEGER division (3): the fraction is lost before the result is stored in the double. Write `7 / 2.0` to get 3.5.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: A `static` local variable is created once and keeps its value between calls: after three calls it is 3. (It is initialised to 0 only the first time.)

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
questions.explain: A variable declared inside `{ }` exists only in that block (its scope). Using it afterwards is a compile error: the name is unknown there.
options: It does not compile: `x` does not exist outside its block
option_notes: The variable is gone after the closing brace.
No default value is involved: the name is not visible at all.
Not even that: the program does not compile.

questions.prompt: What is `sizeof(char)`?
questions.explain: By definition `sizeof(char)` is 1: sizes in C are measured in chars. (A char has `CHAR_BIT` bits, usually 8.) A course quiz may suggest it 'depends on the architecture'; in standard C it never does.
option_notes: Other types vary, but char is the unit of measurement.
`sizeof` counts in chars, not in bits.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the `<stdint.h>` types are true?
questions.explain: The fixed-width types say exactly how many bits they have. The plain `int` only has a minimum size (at least 16 bits); on current Linux systems it happens to be 32.
options: `int32_t` is a signed integer of exactly 32 bits
`uint8_t` is an unsigned integer of 8 bits

questions.prompt: The header that defines `int8_t`, `uint32_t` and the other fixed-width types is `<{{0}}>`.
questions.explain: Include `<stdint.h>` to use `int8_t`, `uint16_t`, `int64_t`, and so on.

questions.prompt: What happens when you assign to a variable declared `const int MAX = 10;` with `MAX = 20;`?
questions.explain: The compiler rejects assignments to `const` objects: that is the whole point of `const`.
options: The program does not compile (assignment of a read-only variable)
MAX stays 10 but there is no error
It compiles and crashes when it runs
option_notes: The compiler reports an error: it does not stay silent.
It is caught at compile time, not at run time.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (Think about how the macro is expanded.)
questions.explain: A macro is TEXT substitution: `SQUARE(2 + 1)` becomes `2 + 1 * 2 + 1`, which is 5 (not 9). Always parenthesise macro parameters: `((x) * (x))`.

questions.prompt: Sort these types into integer types and floating-point types.
questions.explain: `char`, `short`, `long` and `size_t` hold integers; `float` and `double` hold real numbers with a fractional part.

questions.prompt: Match each type with what it is used for.
questions.explain: Each type has a purpose. `size_t` is what `sizeof` returns and is printed with `%zu`; `void` means 'nothing'.
pairs: one character, or a small integer
a floating-point number with about 15 digits
the size of an object, an unsigned integer
no value at all (a function that returns nothing)
a floating-point number with about 6 digits

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (An enum constant without a value continues counting.)
questions.explain: Enum constants count up from the previous one: `B` is `A + 1` = 6, then `C` is set to 1 and `D` follows with 2.

questions.prompt: What can you rely on when a signed `int` goes beyond `INT_MAX` (for example `INT_MAX + 1`)?
questions.explain: Only UNSIGNED arithmetic is defined to wrap around. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour: the compiler may assume it never happens, so do not depend on a result.
options: Nothing: signed overflow is undefined behaviour
The program always stops with an error
option_notes: It often does on real hardware, but the language does not promise it.

questions.prompt: What value does a local variable `int x;` have if you do not initialise it?
questions.explain: A local (automatic) variable has no defined initial value; reading it is undefined behaviour. Only static and global variables start as 0.
options: Indeterminate: using it before assigning is a bug
The value of the last variable that used that memory, guaranteed
option_notes: Only for static or global variables.
It is garbage, but nothing is guaranteed about it.

questions.prompt: A variable declared `static` or at file level and not initialised starts as {{0}}.
questions.explain: Static storage is zero-initialised: numbers are 0 and pointers are NULL.

questions.prompt: What does `static int counter;` mean when it is written at file level (outside any function)?
questions.explain: At file level `static` means internal linkage: other files cannot see the name. Inside a function it means the variable survives between calls.
options: `counter` can only be used in that source file
`counter` keeps its value between function calls (it is a local static)
`counter` can be used from every file of the program
option_notes: That is the meaning inside a function, not at file level.
That is the default WITHOUT static (`extern` linkage).
